I have read 1984, and these are my thoughts:
- The chat/phone listener is damn low, even I set it the highest possible.
- Ok-ish story and plot twist. Maybe I'm too familiar with this kind.
- IT DOES NOT TELL YOU WHEN THE GAME ENDS, SO READ CAREFULLY!
- As far as I know I cannot replay a specific point in the game. I have to replay it from the beginning of the episode.
- The society in this game is nowhere matches the one in Orwell's 1984. You dig every information possible to investigate the case, where in 1984, ALL SURVEILLANCE WERE IN OPERATION, and ALL PEOPLE KNEW ABOUT IT.
- In 1984, if you expressed even the slightest disappointment at the Party's victory news, you had committed Thoughtcrime.
- The endings are duh. There are many unanswered questions at the end.

Conclusion: not recommended.

Very nice narrative driven game where your choices really matter a bit.
I've really enjoyed it and played it to the end (and that is coming from someone who drops games quite easily nowadays).

The game should really use more antialiasing: several aspects of the UI are jagged on the edges.

Now to the real issue: the chat scroll speed is terrifyingly slow (I changed it to the maximum early on, but it was still very, very slow). Even on the first playthrough, waiting for some chats to scroll makes sleeping more entertaining. This eliminates any replayability the game could have.
It is also so easy to fix, I have no idea why the developers don’t do something about this. Maybe they keep this for realism, but it is really shitty gameplay.

In the end, I played this game (without the DLCs) and reached one of its endings. It was an interesting experience. The writing is OK, the plot is interesting enough to keep you playing and the game is not too long.

If you want to replay the game to get all achievements, do not buy unless the developers fix the text scrolling speed issues which other commenters have already pointed out.

The game started quite compelling. It pulled me in with its idea of investigating the public in order to identify those responsible for a series of terror attacks. You must examine: webpages, private chat messages, emails, computer files, and you can even listen in on you're suspects' phone calls. 

As if that wasn't already impressive, the game also contains a system in which false information could cost you the operation. This system causes you to constantly make sure every piece of info is both relevant and correct. 

As you dive deeper into this game you start to see its rather stale side. A major flaw in this surveillance simulator: waiting real time during the targets' phone calls and private messages. You end up losing interest rather easily when you have to sit through these long and dull conversations. I also became quite disappointed when I realized this was all one major mission. It is quite short. I was expecting this to be chock-full of small cases where I must find information on different people for different crimes. Instead, I found myself going through hundreds of pages of the same case. Eventually, I found myself bored and I lost my will to continue. Do not get me wrong, the game is still reasonably fun and it is definitely worth the $2.49 sale tag!

This is my second playthrough, my first on Steam, and I have to say I love everything about this.

The idea behind Orwell, which is inspired by George Orwell the novelist of 1984, highlights many of the themes of Social Injustice, (anti) surveillance, media and control, and how this may affect society in order to 'keep the peace' and reduce any potential threats such as terrorism.

You play the character of an anonymous investigator who collects 'datachunks' in order to formulate a profile against targets who display a potential threat to society. At the beginning you're free to collect whatever information you find on the Target, be that evidence to the case at hand or even private information about their lives. However, later on you find that such actions may lead to interesting consequences.

I have always shared an interest on the themes that the game exposes, as it causes you to question how accurate this game reflects reality. As well as how, as the investigator, it is so easy to exploit the privacy of human beings in order to meet a goal. Is it really for the best interests of the country, to maintain peace? Or is this just a means of surveillance, to find a scapegoat to incriminate against.

Because of Orwell, I've fallen in love with the 'Choice Matter' genre and hope that there is more to come in the future.

The government is spying on its citizens. Don't worry, I'm not about to launch into a rant about the Investigatory Powers Act. Rather, this is the set up to Orwell, a five-part episodic adventure about the tension between privacy and national security. Set in The Nation, Orwell is a visual novel in which you voyeuristically watch over a group of activists—trying to determine who is responsible for a series of bombings.

The titular Orwell is a program for surveilling The Nation's citizens. You play as an investigator, and your job is to analyse the digital footprint of any citizens that The Party has marked as a potential threat. At first you're scouring public and state records—newspapers, websites and police databases. But soon, the intrusion goes deeper. You read emails and chat logs, listen to phone calls, and, in extreme cases, dig through your target's computer.

As you read through the information, the Orwell system will highlight relevant passages of text as data chunks. The system itself is incredibly literal, and unable to distinguishes nuances of language. It can't, for instance, tell that, by listing their current location as 'The Internet', your target is making a funny joke. In fact, if Orwell was analysing that last sentence, it would offer a data chunk saying I thought putting 'The Internet' as your location is a funny joke. It doesn't do sarcasm.

[h1] George Orwell rolls in his grave [/h1]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is an interactive novel exploring the increasingly popular notion that G. Orwell’s iconic “1984” ended up being a guideline for running a country, rather than a warning to its citizens. True to dystopian tones of its inspiration, the title opens up with a bombing attack on a public plaza. Several people were killed, perpetrators are unknown and public is in an uproar. This where you come in, as hand-picked investigator you will use the latest marvel of civil protection technology – Orwell, to solve the case. Orwell “the first and the last line of defence against terrorism” is a powerful software capable of accessing everything connected to the internet. Once a person is authorised by higher-ups for investigation, you are to upload any useful chunks of data into the software and Orwell will process them, granting you access to further information on the target. Person of interest has their phone number on their social media page? Now you can listen to their calls. An e-mail address published on their company’s website? Let’s take a peek inside. Is that a PC id number? You know the drill by now.

[b] Big brother stays vigilant [/b]
With power of Orwell at your fingertips, the player becomes breach of privacy incarnate, yet the decision whether to upload something or not is yours to make. At times you will have conflicting data, that may mislead the authorities acting upon your investigation, while certain details can be ignored altogether. On the other hand, there are also key data chunks that have to be uploaded in order to progress the story and, especially at early stages, there are not a lot of choices to make. Orwell is counterintuitive at first and software’s interpretation of data provided is downright puzzling at times. You better adapt to your new role quickly, as at certain junctions your choices will have an impact at the rest of the story.

It might have drawn your attention that I have addressed the title in question as an “interactive novel”, rather than a game. This is primarily due to the fact that aforementioned limited choice of data chunks thrown into the system is as far as gameplay goes. Alas, it is much easier to regard Orwell as a book, with webpages being equivalent of descriptions and eavesdropped calls and chats being the dialogues. Your investigation quickly unveils a hint of deeply-rooted conspiracy being at work and bombing is but a beginning of something much bigger. Plot divided into 5 chapters thickens quickly and while the general direction of the story is set in stone, your choices can greatly alter fate of certain characters and the ending is yours to twist.

[b] Blessed be the mind too small to question [/b]
Orwell is rather straight-forward with its thought-provoking intent. While the title’s plot unveils in delightfully ambiguous “The Nation”, it doesn’t take a particularly big leap of logic to start drawing parallels. Especially with themes of invigilation, media manipulation and a classic question of “whether the ends justify the means”. As with most of such questions and ideas, Orwell will be whatever you choose to make of it. It won’t be long though, as the title takes roughly 5 hours to complete, making it possible to finish Orwell in a single sitting. That said, the story is divided into coherent chapters of similar length, highlighted by the game as a good moment for a break, should you need one. Orwell is commendable for finding multiple sensible ways to underline impending conclusion of a plot thread, while staying reasonable from in-universe perspective.

Another facet of Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, deserving a separate mention is the art style of the game. Admittedly, the opening cutscene fells remarkably clunky but everything past this very beginning is static images, allowing the style to truly shine. Every picture is built from colourful polygons giving the illustrations believable, yet somewhat obscured, feel to it. Much like the setting of the story, the visuals are deliberately vague, leaving making the parallels up to the player. 

When approached as a book, Orwell makes for enjoyable read with a highly unorthodox mode of delivery. I can easily recommend it to every fan of criminal thriller and political fiction as you should find yourself right at home. If one were to approach the title as a game though, there is very little to speak of. Should you also happen to be the type to skip dialogues in games as a habit, you should probably avoid Orwell like a plague.

P.S. Once you exit Orwell, you are greeted by advertisement of a sequel - Orwell: Ignorance is Strength. Fear not though, Keeping an Eye On You provides a complete storyline, no “to be continued” ending attached.

One of the game’s themes is how people present themselves online as well as offline. This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other in the game. Cassandra Watergate is, on one hand, an emotionally unstable, childish woman who does not care about adult responsibility, but on the other hand she is an activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police.

Which character is the real one? That is what makes the story interesting. Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are. People are different online and in the presence of other people. Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to make the player want to continue playing.

The gameplay itself is quite easy and straight-forward. You use Orwell to find data on various people supposedly involved in terrorist activities, in order to uncover who's responsible and who's not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue. Orwell might be easy, but that does not make it any less interesting. Simple, but very polished.
